title: Tulpat piti uusia
subtitle: The spark plugs had to be replaced

blocks.text: Back in Lesson 3 you saw ongelmia ei ilmennyt — 'no problems appeared' — without stopping on that -ia ending. Reviewers rarely complain about just one thing: parts, faults, and problems come in groups. This lesson gives you Finnish plurals, plus a new use of a word you already know: pitää.

blocks.annotated: {Tulpat|grammar|nominative plural|the spark plugs} {piti|grammar|impersonal past|had to be} uusia.
blocks.translation: The spark plugs had to be replaced.

blocks.title: Plural complaints, plural evidence
blocks.text: When a Finnish reviewer lists osat, viat, or tulpat in the plural, it reads as more damning than a single singular complaint — it signals a pattern, not a one-off mistake. Watch for plurals doing quiet rhetorical work in the harsher reviews in this corpus.

blocks.content: The simplest Finnish plural just adds {-t|grammar|nominative plural suffix|-s} to the end of the word. Osa (part) → {osat|grammar|nominative plural|the parts}. Tulppa (spark plug) → {tulpat|grammar|nominative plural|the spark plugs} — note the double p softens to single p, a small sound-shift called consonant gradation that you'll meet more of later. Vika (fault) → {viat|grammar|nominative plural|the faults}.

You've already used the partitive plural without knowing it: ongelmia ei ilmennyt (Lesson 3) is 'no problems appeared', with {ongelmia|grammar|partitive plural|problems} taking -ia. This shape appears after negation, after quantity words, and any time you mean 'some of' rather than 'all of' the group. Osa → {osia|grammar|partitive plural|parts, some of}.

blocks.title: The other meaning of pitää
blocks.text: From Lesson 2 you know piti paikkansa, 'held true' — from pitää meaning 'to hold'. But pitää has a second, completely different everyday meaning: 'must/have to'. In the past, that becomes {piti|grammar|impersonal past + infinitive|had to}, always paired with a plain infinitive verb: tulpat piti uusia, 'the spark plugs had to be renewed'. Same word, different job — context tells you which.

items.fi: Tulpat {piti|grammar|impersonal past + infinitive|had to be} uusia.
items.en: The spark plugs had to be replaced.

items.fi: Auto {piti|grammar|impersonal past + infinitive|had to be} jäähdytellä.
items.en: The car had to be left to cool down.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: You don't need to master every plural type today. Just learn to notice the two shapes: a plain -t at the end means 'the [things]' as a group (osat, viat, tulpat); an -a/-ä turning into -ia/-iä usually means 'some [things]', often right after ei. Spot the shape, and the meaning follows.

blocks.content: Tulpat: TUL-pat (short, crisp — the single 'p' after the plural -t is the gradation Lesson mentioned). Osat: O-sat (two even syllables). Ongelmia: ON-gel-mi-a (four syllables, same soft 'g' as ongelma).

rows.en: the spark plugs (nominative plural of tulppa)
parts, some of (partitive plural of osa)
